entities.summary:
Bérenger de Landore (1262–1330), a scion of a noble family from Salmiech in southern France, rose to prominence as a leading figure within the Dominican Order and the medieval Church. His career trajectory saw him serve as the Master of the Order of Preachers from 1312 to 1317, a pivotal period marked by the aftermath of the Knights Templar suppression and the Avignon Papacy. He subsequently held the prestigious and politically charged office of Archbishop of Santiago de Compostela from 1317 until his death in 1330, wielding significant ecclesiastical and temporal authority in the Kingdom of Galicia.

During his mastership of the Dominican Order, Bérenger navigated complex internal and external pressures. He oversaw the order's intellectual and missionary activities, ensuring its continued influence across Europe and beyond, while also managing its extensive network of convents and schools. His tenure coincided with the pontificate of Pope Clement V and later Pope John XXII, necessitating careful diplomacy regarding papal directives and the broader political landscape of the early 14th century. As Archbishop of Santiago, he was a powerful feudal lord and a key patron of the pilgrimage route, responsible for the spiritual welfare of pilgrims and the administration of vast diocesan lands, often clashing with local nobility and even the Castilian crown over jurisdictional rights.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bérenger de Landore held two powerful positions—Master of the Dominicans and Archbishop of Santiago—at a critical juncture for the medieval Church, allowing him to shape both a major religious order and a significant pilgrimage center. His administrative work contributed to the stability and influence of these institutions in the early 14th century.
